edits.old: Indoor inspection, monitoring, and emergency-response missions are representative examples. A MAV can enter confined spaces and cross passages whose clearance is only a few rotor radii. It can approach machinery, beams, pipes, and damaged structures that would otherwise require shutting down a facility or exposing an operator to danger. These missions are also among the most demanding. Satellite positioning is generally unavailable, onboard sensing and computation are limited, and communication can be degraded by the surrounding structure. At the same time, obstacle avoidance leaves little room for tracking errors. The boundaries therefore become part of the aerodynamic environment rather than passive geometric constraints: the wakes generated by the propellers interact with nearby surfaces and alter the forces and moments acting on the vehicle.

remarks.text: My general comment, as having read only the intro so far, is that the text is quite ok but sometimes vague and uses improper wording, sometimes is a bit long/repetitive and has a relatively weak literature review on the problem of ground effect identification
Literature coverage of GE modeling and, above all, of identification is thin

The ground-effect literature is too narrow for the physical claims made. Missing work on partial ground effect, finite surfaces, dynamic ground effect, multirotor recirculation, and learned ground-effect compensation directly bears on the model chosen here.

The current paragraph (line 45) covers the classical model and two multirotor studies only. The literature on *how GE parameters are obtained* splits into test-stand fits (most multirotor work), analytical/image models, CFD, learned models from flight data, and observer-based estimates. None of the works found designs flights to identify GE parameters. That is the gap to state, and it is defensible.

Two 2026 Vertical Flight Society papers are directly relevant to the obstacle-edge model and were not in either earlier review. **Yon and Li (2026)** correlate partial-coverage rotor thrust with a circular-segment rotor-ground overlap area, which is essentially your $\chi_i$. **Herz et al. (2026)** fly a quadrotor over a building-like edge and find that full GE develops only after most of the vehicle has crossed it, with the airframe driving the onset. Cite the first at Eq. (corrected-thrust) as support and the second as a limitation.

**Missing citation.** "since the middle of the twentieth century" and "the Cheeseman-Bennett approximation" are uncited, although `\cite{CheesemanBennett1955}` exists and is first used at L529. The wake-turning physics needs [CITE: rotorcraft aerodynamics textbook]. **Improper word, to check.** "Classical momentum-theory relations, including the Cheeseman-Bennett approximation" is doubtful because Cheeseman and Bennett used the method of images. The cited report is also titled *The Effect of Ground on a Helicopter Rotor in Forward Flight*, while the text says "hovering". "lift" for a rotor should be "thrust". **Vague.** "primarily through its normalized clearance" does not say normalized by what. "clearance alone is insufficient" does not say for what. **Logic.** P4 stresses that "velocity changes the response" (Kan), but II-B L544 says velocity dependence "is limited over the low-speed range considered here". State the advance-ratio range once and reconcile the two (see IIB-9). **Grammar.** "Cheeseman-Bennett" should use an en-dash, `Cheeseman--Bennett`.

The first covers the classical model and multirotor models with how their parameters were obtained, and puts the Crazyflie result of Carter et al. next to the nonmonotonic responses reported recently. The second covers partial coverage at edges and dynamic effects, which bear directly on your overlap weighting and static law. The third covers identification and compensation in control, and ends on the gap: no study selects flights by their information on the GE parameters. Kan et al. now support "GE varies with speed" in general; the low-speed range of this paper is handled at Sec. II-B ([[C35]]). 22 references, 21 of them new.

edits.old: Ground effect (GE), by contrast, has been investigated since the middle of the twentieth century in classical aviation and rotorcraft. An underlying surface changes the pressure field and redirects the rotor wake radially, reducing the induced velocity and induced power required for a given lift. This can improve aerodynamic efficiency during takeoff, hover, and low-altitude flight. Classical momentum-theory relations, including the Cheeseman-Bennett approximation, describe the effect for an isolated rotor hovering above an extended plane primarily through its normalized clearance. At MAV scale, however, four nearby rotors interact with one another and with the central body, while low Reynolds number and wake recirculation make the response vehicle dependent~\cite{Matus2020,Carter2021}. Forward motion adds wake convection and a finite residence time over the surface. Kan et al.~\cite{Kan2019} confirmed the expected efficiency gain for small multirotors in forward flight, but also showed that clearance alone is insufficient and that velocity changes the response.
edits.new:
Ground effect (GE), by contrast, has been studied since the 1950s for helicopter rotors. A surface below the rotor redirects the wake radially and reduces the induced velocity and the power required for a given thrust. Cheeseman and Bennett derived the resulting thrust gain of an isolated rotor from its clearance-to-radius ratio and forward speed~\cite{CheesemanBennett1955}, and rotor experiments showed that the near-ground flow changes regime with advance ratio and depends on translational acceleration~\cite{Curtiss1984}. In multirotors, rotor--rotor interaction and the flow beneath the central body change this response~\cite{Matus2020}. It has been described by adding image rotors and an empirical body coefficient to the classical model~\cite{SanchezCuevas2017}, or by exponential, quasi-steady, and Gaussian-process models of the measured thrust~\cite{He2019,HeLeang2020,Franzetti2024ICUAS}. On a tethered Crazyflie~2.0, the near-ground lift increase exceeded twice the classical prediction~\cite{Carter2021}, whereas experiments and computations on other quadrotors report a nonmonotonic thrust or power response near one to one and a half rotor radii~\cite{Tanabe2021,Lei2026}.

Flight near obstacles adds two complications. First, the surface may lie under only some of the rotors. The resulting thrust imbalance produces a moment that a cascaded PID controller rejects poorly~\cite{SanchezCuevas2017}. For a single rotor, the thrust under partial coverage has been correlated with the overlap area between rotor disk and surface~\cite{Yon2026}. Free-flight tests near a building-like edge, however, found that full GE develops only after most of the vehicle has crossed the edge~\cite{Herz2026}. Second, GE is not static. It varies with forward and climb speed~\cite{Kan2019,HeLeang2025} and with the motion of the surface~\cite{He2024}, and dynamic quadrotor tests have complemented the static characterizations~\cite{DelContBernard2017}.

Control studies compensate GE online or learn it from flight data. Adaptive control~\cite{Wei2019} and disturbance observers~\cite{He2019,LiX2024} counter the near-ground force, and Li et al.~\cite{LiX2024} also fitted a GE model to observer estimates recorded in hovering flights. Deep networks trained on flight data~\cite{Shi2019} and richer models that include surface motion and past states~\cite{He2024} or GE torques and rotor drag~\cite{Yang2025} provide feedforward or model-based compensation. In aircraft, GE coefficients have been identified from flight data recorded without dedicated maneuvers~\cite{Vitale2010}. Flight-vehicle system identification, by contrast, designs the inputs to maximize the information on the unknown parameters~\cite{Mehra1974,Jategaonkar2015,Morelli2016}. Robot trajectories have been synthesized to maximize the Fisher information~\cite{Wilson2014}, and informative trajectories have been planned for other multirotor parameters~\cite{Bahnemann2017}. To our knowledge, no study has selected the flights of a multirotor by their information on the GE parameters.

items.title: Paragraph 5: why the interaction must be predicted

remarks.text: My general comment, as having read only the intro so far, is that the text is quite ok but sometimes vague and uses improper wording, sometimes is a bit long/repetitive and has a relatively weak literature review on the problem of ground effect identification

**Vague referent.** "These limitations" could mean the classical models or the MAV-scale effects. **Vague.** "the purpose of an aerodynamic model is not only to reproduce a force measurement" is negative framing without a positive statement. **Grammar.** "compensating the interaction" should be "compensating for the interaction". **Improper word.** "The problem is especially clear over finite obstacles" uses "clear" for "explicit" or "acute". **Repetition.** R3 with P6.

items.why: "These limitations" pointed to the old paragraph; the new opening follows from the gap stated just before. The negative framing ("not only to reproduce") becomes a positive statement, "safe path" becomes "collision-free path", and "especially clear" becomes "explicit".

edits.old: These limitations matter in cluttered flight because the purpose of an aerodynamic model is not only to reproduce a force measurement. The vehicle must remain on a safe path while moving from one obstacle to the next. A thrust variation above one surface can produce a small vertical excursion that appears benign locally but consumes the clearance available at a following beam, ceiling, or doorway. Predicting and compensating the interaction before the tracking error develops is therefore a safety requirement. The problem is especially clear over finite obstacles, where the vehicle enters GE, remains in it briefly, and then crosses a trailing edge. Leading-edge exposure, transient wake development, and post-obstacle recovery all occur within one mission.
edits.new: Accurate GE prediction matters in cluttered flight because an aerodynamic model must do more than reproduce a measured force. It must let the controller keep the vehicle on a collision-free path from one obstacle to the next. A thrust change above one surface can produce a vertical excursion that is harmless locally but uses up the clearance available at a following beam, ceiling, or doorway. The interaction must therefore be predicted and compensated for before a tracking error develops. Finite obstacles make this requirement explicit. The vehicle enters GE, remains in it briefly, and then crosses a trailing edge, so leading-edge exposure, transient wake development, and post-obstacle recovery all occur within one mission.

**Unsupported.** "Most MAVs rely on cascaded proportional-integral-derivative (PID) loops" has no citation. **Vague.** "robust nominal behavior". **Colon.** "intrinsically reactive: an unmodeled disturbance ..." **Redundant.** "the computational burden related to its online computation". **Improper word.** "a confidently wrong correction" is informal. The control literature is also incomplete. Since the experiment repeatedly executes the same spatial mission and learns a feedforward/reference correction, iterative learning control and learned residual dynamics are important comparators, not optional background.

items.why: Removes the colon, "intrinsically", "confidently wrong" and "micro drone", and adds a quadrotor reference for MPC with learned residual dynamics, the closest MPC variant to the learning in this paper. "MPC" is not used again, so the acronym goes.

edits.old: Their low computational cost and robust nominal behavior make them well suited to small onboard processors. However, they are intrinsically reactive: an unmodeled disturbance must first produce an error before feedback counters it. Close to an obstacle, this delay can consume the available safety margin.
edits.new: They are cheap to compute and robust near their nominal operating point, which suits small onboard processors. However, they are reactive. An unmodeled disturbance must first produce an error before feedback counters it, and close to an obstacle this delay can consume the available safety margin.

edits.old: Model-based predictive methods can instead modify the command or reference before the disturbance fully develops. Model predictive control (MPC), in particular, offers a systematic way to optimize future behavior while accounting for dynamics and constraints~\cite{MPCReview2021}. Its effectiveness is nevertheless tied to the model used for prediction and the computational burden related to its online computation. An incomplete model can generate a confidently wrong correction, whereas a more faithful aerodynamic model may be difficult to identify and too expensive to optimize repeatedly on the limited hardware of a micro drone.
edits.new: Predictive methods instead modify the command or reference before the disturbance develops. Model predictive control optimizes future behavior while accounting for dynamics and constraints~\cite{MPCReview2021}, also on quadrotors with learned residual dynamics~\cite{Torrente2021}. Its effectiveness depends on the prediction model and on the cost of solving the optimization online. An incomplete model can produce a wrong correction, whereas a more faithful aerodynamic model may be difficult to identify and too expensive to optimize repeatedly on the limited hardware of a MAV.

edits.old:
The actions carried out in each block can be summarized as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Policy deployment: the iteration starts from the parameters selected at the end of the previous DT evaluation. The first interaction uses the baseline policy $\pi_{\mathrm{BL}}$, executed through the built-in PID controller, and provides the reference performance for comparison with the optimized policies. For $e_n=1$, the deployed policy is an information-oriented policy $\pi_{\iota}(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\iota}^{(n)})$; for $e_n=0$, it is a performance-oriented policy $\pi_{\bullet}(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\pi}^{(n)})$. This first block converts a design decision made in the DT into an executable command for the physical controller. The policy representation, its admissible parameter set, and all safety checks are application dependent, but the RT principle is unchanged: the DT proposes the interaction, while the physical environment supplies the evidence that determines whether the proposal was useful.
    \item Physical episode: the physical environment evolves under its hidden dynamics, the deployed policy, and the exogenous input $\mathbf d$. The latter collects quantities that influence the episode without being selected by the policy, such as environmental disturbances, initial-condition variations, or changes in available actuation. The internal state $\mathbf s_{\bullet}$ is not generally known. RT receives the noisy observations $\mathbf o_{\bullet}$, the commanded inputs, and the operating conditions that are needed to reconstruct the episode. This distinction is essential because the DT is updated from what the experiment can actually measure.
    \item Recording: the observations, deployed policy, operating condition, control signals, exogenous inputs, and evaluated physical reward are collected in the episode record $\mathcal E^{(n)}$ and appended to the replay buffer $\mathcal B$. The purpose of this passage is to preserve a common, traceable description of the interaction before the information and performance branches use it differently. The replay buffer therefore links all later virtual operations to the experiment that produced their data and permits a model update to be repeated on the complete cumulative dataset.
    \item Factual replay: the DT reconstructs the initial state and replays the recorded policy under the measured operating conditions. When $e_n=1$, DT observations $\mathbf o_{\circ}$ are compared with $\mathbf o_{\bullet}$ and the mismatch is differentiated through the closed-loop twin. The model parameters are then updated from $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m)}$ to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m+1)}$ using the cumulative replay buffer. When $e_n=0$, the model parameters remain frozen, so that $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m+1)}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m)}$. The new policy-reward pair bypasses identification and instead augments the dataset used to learn the reward-transfer surrogate. Factual replay thus has a different learning target in the two phases, while the recorded evidence entering the loop remains the same.
    \item Virtual candidate evaluation: with the current model parameters, the DT evaluates interactions that have not yet been carried out. In the information branch, information-oriented policies are propagated through the closed-loop model, differentiated with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p$, and scored by the information they are expected to add to the weakest parameter direction. In the performance branch, the converged DT first provides the model-based policy $\pi_{\mathrm{MB}}$. Candidate deviations around this policy are then simulated, rejected if they violate the DT safety checks, and assigned both a DT reward and a reward-transfer surrogate prediction of their physical reward. This block is the main computational advantage of RT: a large candidate set can be explored in the DT while only a small number of selected policies reaches the physical environment.
    \item Choice of the next interaction: the final block converts the virtual evaluations into the next physical policy. For $e_n=1$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:rt-e-optimal} selects the candidate that maximizes the smallest eigenvalue of the cumulative Fisher matrix and therefore strengthens the least-observed joint parameter direction. For $e_n=0$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:rt-next-performance} selects the candidate with the largest Expected Improvement, balancing a high predicted physical reward against uncertainty in the learned transfer. The selected parameters are returned to Block~1, the physical episode index advances from $n$ to $n+1$, and the loop repeats. In the present work, the model-update index $m$ advances only in the information phase; separating the two indices makes clear that collecting a new performance episode does not imply a new model update.
\end{enumerate}

The selector value is scheduled within the test campaign. The loop first repeats Blocks~1-6 with $e_n=1$ until the model satisfies the adopted convergence and uncertainty criteria. It then switches once to $e_n=0$ and keeps the identified parameters fixed while the reward-transfer surrogate is refined. The following subsection specializes every element of this generic loop for the adopted test case.

The blocks of Fig.~\ref{fig:rt_framework} perform the following operations.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Policy deployment. The policy selected in the previous iteration is deployed; the first episode uses the baseline policy $\pi_{\mathrm{BL}}$, which sets the reference performance.
    \item Physical episode. The physical environment evolves under its hidden dynamics, the deployed policy, and the exogenous input $\mathbf d$, and returns the noisy observations $\mathbf o_{\bullet}$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:rt-physical-observation}.
    \item Recording. The record $\mathcal E^{(n)}$ is appended to the replay buffer $\mathcal B$, so that every model update uses the complete dataset.
    \item Factual replay. For $e_n=1$, the DT replays the recorded episode, and the mismatch between $\mathbf o_{\circ}$ and $\mathbf o_{\bullet}$ updates $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m)}$ to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p^{(m+1)}$. For $e_n=0$, the model stays frozen, and the new policy--reward pair enters the reward-transfer surrogate.
    \item Virtual candidate evaluation. The DT simulates candidate policies. Information-oriented candidates are scored by their predicted information on $\boldsymbol{\theta}_p$. Performance-oriented candidates around $\pi_{\mathrm{MB}}$ that pass the DT checks receive a DT reward and a surrogate prediction of their physical reward. Many candidates are evaluated virtually, but only the selected one is flown.
    \item Choice of the next interaction. Equation~\eqref{eq:rt-e-optimal} ($e_n=1$) or Eq.~\eqref{eq:rt-next-performance} ($e_n=0$) selects the next policy, $n$ advances to $n+1$, and the loop returns to Block~1.
\end{enumerate}

edits.old: Only two condition-specific EI iterations are used here, so the result is interpreted as a proof-of-concept local extension of the RT workflow rather than as convergence of a general surrogate. At a new operating condition, the local DT first supplies a model-based policy that already improves substantially over the baseline policy. When direct transfer fails to improve that policy, a small number of physical interactions can reveal how the GP discrepancy has changed and redirect the search toward a better condition-specific solution. sources.text: Lowest measured mean clearance over the obstacle: 0.68R (INF_09). Information design admitted a DT lowest-rotor clearance of 0.3R (`informative_policy.py:68`).

edits.old: This work demonstrated Reinforcement Twinning for predictive trajectory control of a micro aerial vehicle crossing a finite obstacle in ground effect. The information phase provided evidence that the designed experiments added more than visual diversity: the cumulative smallest Fisher eigenvalue grew much faster than for repeated baseline experiments, and restricting the design from the broad domain to the near-wall domain restored information gain as the former began to saturate. Although the identified model parameters remained correlated, the resulting ground-effect function was well constrained over the control-relevant clearance range. Parameter decorrelation was therefore not treated as the objective by itself; the relevant outcome was the improved identification of the weakest observable parameter direction and of the aerodynamic correction used by the controller.
edits.new: This work demonstrated Reinforcement Twinning for the trajectory control of a micro aerial vehicle crossing a finite obstacle in ground effect. In the information phase, the designed experiments raised the smallest eigenvalue of the cumulative Fisher-information proxy to $3.242$ over the baseline and twelve information-oriented episodes, against $0.387$ for the baseline record repeated over the same episodes. The near-wall records, two of them archived, gave most of this increase. The parameters remain correlated ($\rho_{A,p}=0.818$), but the uncertainty indicator of $f_{\mathrm{GE}}$ fell to $15\%$ at $z/R=1$ and $4.3\%$ at $z/R=1.5$.

edits.old: Model-based optimization remained the backbone of the framework. The identified DT generated an anticipatory model-based policy that improved tracking without replacing the onboard feedback controller and while satisfying the adopted virtual safety constraints. The remaining replay error then motivated the performance phase rather than invalidating the DT. Fractional and Sobol policies calibrated the reward-transfer surrogate, while Expected Improvement directed subsequent physical experiments toward uncertain and potentially better policies. With few additional interactions, the resulting $\pi_{\mathrm{EI}}^{\star}$ outperformed the model-based policy by compensating for response features that the low-order static model could not rank accurately. In this way, the DT restricted the search to a screened, high-performing neighborhood, and physical rewards were used specifically to learn the GP discrepancy within that neighborhood.
edits.new: The DT produced a model-based policy that raised the physical reward from $0.544$ to $0.855$, kept the onboard feedback controller, and passed the DT clearance checks. Interpolation and Sobol policies then calibrated the reward-transfer surrogate, and after nine EI-selected policies the search found a policy with physical reward $0.952$, mainly by reducing the post-obstacle undershoot that the static model does not predict.

edits.old: The conclusions are therefore limited to the tested envelope. The ground-effect model represents an unsteady rotor-surface interaction with a static two-parameter law and cannot reproduce every transient feature. The physical experiments were constrained to $z/R\geq0.5$, so the results do not support extrapolation toward contact, and generalization was examined at only two additional operating conditions. Future work should extend the campaign across a denser velocity-clearance domain, account explicitly for repeated-measurement uncertainty in the reward-transfer surrogate, and investigate richer unsteady aerodynamic models, moving landing surfaces, and onboard or real-time policy adaptation. Within the present limits, the campaign shows how RT can combine interpretable physics, virtual safety screening, and a targeted data-driven correction to improve control performance without requiring unconstrained model-free exploration.
edits.new: The results are limited to a static two-parameter ground-effect law, to the clearances flown (the lowest measured mean clearance over the obstacle was $0.68R$), and to two off-nominal conditions. Admissibility was checked only in the DT, which underpredicts the trailing-edge undershoot, so the DT screening reduces the risk of a policy without bounding it. Future work should cover a denser velocity--clearance domain, include repeated-measurement uncertainty in the surrogate, and test unsteady aerodynamic models, moving landing surfaces, and onboard or real-time policy adaptation.
